title: Transshipment Crackdowns Won’t Fix the U.S.-China Trade Imbalance
gist: The White House's August 2026 'Great Transshipment Scam' report stretches transshipment to cover legitimate third-country manufacturing with Chinese inputs. CSIS's HS-6 overlap analysis finds rerouting growing only in a few economies such as Cambodia and Laos, and argues the persistent U.S.-China imbalance reflects macro fundamentals (China's export model, the U.S. AI investment boom, low U.S. savings) plus 10-20 point tariff differentials that pull production into connector economies, so enforcement alone will not fix it.

themes.theme: Chinese value added via connector economies

insights.claim: Chinese value added entering the U.S. has grown since 2018 even as direct U.S. imports from China fell, with Mexico and Vietnam carrying 23 percent and 15 percent respectively of indirect Chinese value added in 2024, per a 2026 Peterson Institute brief.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Mexico and Vietnam are the most exposed to U.S. pressure over Chinese content in their exports.
insights.locator: The first part of the White House’s

insights.claim: A 2026 Federal Reserve study found Chinese production in Mexico accounted for about 14 points of Mexico's export gains after the 2018-19 tariffs, while direct transshipment accounted for less than 1 point.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Chinese FDI into Mexican manufacturing, not rerouting, is the main channel, making it the likely next target of U.S. rules-of-origin tightening.
insights.quote: Chinese production in Mexico accounted for about 14 points of Mexico’s export gains after the 2018–19 tariffs, while direct transshipment accounted for less than 1 point

insights.claim: Conventional transshipment explains only a subset of Chinese-origin value added reaching the U.S.; the rest flows through substantial transformation in multistage supply chains driven by Chinese outbound investment, firms relocating from China and local firms using Chinese inputs.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Crackdowns on fraud will not materially change aggregate Chinese content in U.S. imports.

themes.theme: Empirical test of transshipment by HS-6 overlap

insights.claim: CSIS's Finger-Kreinin export similarity analysis for 2024-2026 shows the overlap between Chinese imports and U.S.-bound exports has not meaningfully grown for many economies named in the White House report.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Challenges the premise that transshipment is the dominant evasion channel justifying broad tariff enforcement.

insights.claim: Cambodia and Laos, and to a lesser extent Singapore and Indonesia, show rising overlap between Chinese imports and U.S.-bound exports, particularly in photovoltaic cells and steel products already subject to Commerce Department circumvention probes.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Solar and steel flows from these countries are most at risk of new anti-circumvention duties.

insights.claim: Malaysia, Mexico, Thailand and Vietnam show no rise in overlapping trade, and Malaysia and Thailand show declines, because they import simple electronics components from China and export advanced electronics to the U.S.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Electronics supply chains in Southeast Asia reflect genuine value addition, reducing the case for punitive measures against them.

insights.claim: Misreported value, classification or origin has spiked since new China tariffs in early 2025, with products such as tungsten carbide, quartz, plastic bags and batteries found in illicit rerouting schemes.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Importers in these product categories face heightened enforcement and penalty risk.

insights.claim: Transshipment is not inherently illegal, as companies route goods through third countries for port access, logistics synergies and storage, and the White House report conflates legitimate business with criminal behavior.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Overbroad enforcement could penalize legitimate logistics and supply chain operations.
insights.quote: By branding all such undesirable activity as illegal, the White House report conflates entirely legitimate business actions with criminal behavior.

themes.theme: Macro drivers of the U.S.-China imbalance

insights.claim: China's export-oriented growth model, with an undervalued real exchange rate, tepid consumer spending and state support for tech sectors, diverts blocked U.S. exports elsewhere rather than curbing production.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Expect continued Chinese export surges into third markets, fueling trade friction in Europe and elsewhere.

insights.claim: In 2025 China's total exports rose 5.5 percent even as exports to the U.S. fell about 20 percent, with many displaced exports shifting to the European Union.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Rising Chinese export pressure on the EU raises odds of European trade defense measures.
insights.quote: Data from 2025 shows that China’s total exports rose 5.5 percent even as its exports to the United States fell about 20 percent

insights.claim: The U.S. AI infrastructure investment surge, combined with low household savings and a widening fiscal deficit, pulls in foreign capital and depresses the trade balance.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The AI capex boom structurally widens the U.S. trade deficit regardless of tariff policy.

insights.claim: AI spending has pushed up U.S. imports both directly from China, which dominates manufacturing of electrical transformers and optical transceivers, and from connector economies reliant on Chinese supply chains.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: AI data center buildout depends on Chinese-made grid and optical components, a tariff and supply risk for hyperscaler capex.
insights.locator: Inverse factors contribute to the persistent

insights.claim: U.S. tariffs since 2025 have shifted supply chain contours but not reduced underlying U.S.-China trade imbalances.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Tariffs are reshaping trade geography rather than trade balances, favoring connector-economy manufacturing.

themes.theme: Tariff differentials as the real driver

insights.claim: Many connector economies now face average statutory U.S. tariff rates 10 to 20 percentage points or more below China's, creating strong incentives to relocate operations even where it otherwise makes little economic sense.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Tariff arbitrage is a key driver of FDI into Southeast Asia and Mexico and will persist while differentials last.

insights.claim: Footprint shifts in response to tariff differentials arise from decentralized profit-maximizing behavior, not a central Chinese government plan to circumvent tariffs.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Rebuts the coordinated-evasion narrative underpinning aggressive enforcement.

themes.theme: Policy outlook: rules of origin and enforcement

insights.claim: The White House's proposed 'AI Detective Border' enforcement apparatus will require more customs spending, higher corporate compliance costs and stronger monitoring demands on trading partners.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Rising compliance costs for importers; potential demand for trade-compliance and customs-analytics technology.

insights.claim: Much of the White House critique targets practices like component integration that CBP has often ruled constitute substantial transformation, and its tests such as Chinese input share or ownership have not historically determined origin.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Enforcement without rule changes will face legal limits; watch for rules-of-origin renegotiation.

insights.claim: All 10 reciprocal trade agreements finalized so far include placeholder clauses letting a party set new rules of origin if benefits accrue substantially to third countries, and the ongoing USMCA negotiations may provide a template.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: USMCA review outcome is the leading indicator for stricter origin rules that could hit Chinese-invested factories in Mexico and Asia.

insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Lower VAT rebates raise effective export costs for Chinese battery and solar makers, pressuring margins.
